scaffold_items.statement: Home robot adoption is concentrated in floor cleaning, while broader household robot use remains less established.
Some adults already own robot vacuums.
Some adults already own robot vacuums with AI features, although this is a different measure from general robot vacuum ownership.
Interest in robots that help with chores extends beyond established ownership, but interest alone is not proof of adoption.
Some robot vacuums can recognize obstacles and move selected objects with a mechanical arm when configured through an app.
Mobile home robots are being developed for laundry, bed making, and tidying, with remote assistance available when needed.
The announced prices and payment plans for some mobile home robots are reservation terms, not evidence of completed mass-market sales.
Rollouts of new home robots are planned to begin in limited regions before broader national availability.
A mobile home robot still needs regular charging and dedicated floor space, and its working time depends on the task and load.
Robot vacuums remain mainly suited to routine floor cleaning and can underperform manual vacuums on some surfaces; they do not cover stairs or ceilings.
Deep cleaning remains a limitation, especially in less suitable rooms or on challenging surfaces.
Reliable avoidance of cords, pet waste, and other household obstacles is still not taken for granted.
During an automation trial, manual cleaning fell while cleaning became more frequent and total cleaning activity increased.
Research estimates link robot vacuum use with less housework time, while not finding a clear change in sleep time.
The link between robot vacuum use and work participation remains associative rather than proof that the robot caused the change.
Robot vacuum owners can report high satisfaction even when their device does not fully replace manual cleaning.
Research robots have learned a broad set of household tasks from brief human demonstrations and model adaptation in real homes.
These results show research feasibility, not the performance of a consumer general-purpose household robot.
A research system can learn individual dishwashing steps from a human demonstration.
Completing the whole dishwashing task remains unreliable in research settings, and this does not show that mass-market products are available.
A humanoid robot has demonstrated autonomous laundry folding in a controlled demonstration.
The demonstration does not establish reliable performance with varied household clothing or practical mass production.
Home robot development is moving beyond vacuuming toward mobile machines with dexterous hands, sensing, and links to household appliances for household chores.
Broader home robots remain at the announcement or demonstration stage, without established consumer pricing, mass production, or independent home evaluation.
Research is moving toward general-purpose home robots that combine language, vision, planning, physical action, feedback, and adaptation in open-ended home environments.
